query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, low‐level aluminum additions control phase stability by inducing local lattice distortions and short‐range chemical ordering that lower the free energy difference between the FCC matrix and competing phases. This metastable FCC state is then able to activate transformation-induced plasticity (via deformation twinning or an FCC-to-hcp transition) under cryogenic loading and inhibit defect accumulation under high-temperature and irradiation conditions, thereby concurrently enhancing high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy with negligible Al content exhibiting a single-phase FCC structure and moderate lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Incrementally increase the Al content (e.g., 5–10 at% Al) while keeping the Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni concentrations nearly equiatomic.
generation.conditions: Identical thermomechanical processing with subsequent mechanical testing over a wide temperature range (cryogenic to high temperature), under oxidative environments and controlled irradiation exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: Al-induced lattice distortion and local chemical short-range ordering that modify stacking fault energies and the free energy landscape between FCC and alternative phases (such as hcp).
generation.mechanism: The larger atomic radius and ordering tendency of Al atoms introduce local strains that disrupt dislocation motion and lower the barrier for deformation twinning or phase transformation upon mechanical loading. These changes also help to suppress defect coalescence under irradiation and stabilize a protective passive film against environmental attack, yielding a balanced combination of properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with optimal low-level Al additions will exhibit a metastable FCC matrix that under stress triggers transformation-induced plasticity (e.g., twinning or limited FCC-to-hcp transformation), resulting in enhanced yield strength at high temperatures, improved ductility and toughness at cryogenic temperatures, better resistance to environmental oxidation, and reduced radiation-induced defect accumulation relative to the alloy without Al.
generation.baseline: The Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA without Al, which shows a stable FCC structure but with less effective activation of deformation mechanisms under extreme temperatures and irradiation, and consequently reduced high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated only for near-equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with controlled low-level Al additions; excessive Al (e.g., >10 at%) may lead to excessive lattice distortion and promote the formation of brittle intermetallic phases.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Al concentration and the relative contributions of lattice distortion versus chemical ordering in stabilizing the desired metastable phase remain to be quantified experimentally, and may be sensitive to processing routes.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with varying Al contents (0, 5, 10, and 15 at%) under identical processing conditions. Characterize their phase structures via X-ray diffraction and high-resolution electron microscopy, then subject the alloys to tensile testing at cryogenic and high temperatures, corrosion tests in oxidative environments, and irradiation experiments under controlled conditions.
measurements: Phase fraction analysis (quantifying FCC vs hcp or other phases)
Microstructural observations (degree of deformation twinning, lattice distortion, and defect clustering)
Mechanical properties (yield strength, tensile strength, and ductility at various temperatures)
Environmental resistance (corrosion/passivation behavior at high temperatures)
Radiation tolerance (defect density and irradiation hardening measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of low-level Al does not lead to a measurable shift in the phase balance (e.g., no increase in transformation-induced twinning or FCC-to-hcp transformation under stress) and fails to improve the alloy's high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, or cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline (Al-free) alloy—or if increased Al content consistently produces brittle intermetallic phases with degraded properties—the proposed mechanism is falsified.

AlxCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloys Enable Simultaneous Electrical and Mechanical Robustness at Thermoelectric Interfaces

Abstract: AbstractThe interface between high-performance thermoelectric materials and electrodes critically governs the conversion efficiency and long-term reliability of thermoelectric generators under high-temperature operation. Here, we propose AlxCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (HEA) as barrier layers to bond Cu-W electrodes with p-type skutterudite (p-SKD) thermoelectric materials. The HEA/p-SKD interface exhibited excellent chemical bonding with a stable and controllable reaction layer, forming a dense, defect-free (Fe,Ni,Co,Cr)Sb phase (thickness of ~2.5 μm) at the skutterudites side. The interfacial resistivity achieved a low value of 0.26 μΩ·cm2 and remained at 7.15 μΩ·cm2 after aging at 773 K for 16 days. Moreover, the interface demonstrated remarkable mechanical stability, with an initial shear strength of 88 MPa. After long-term aging for 16 days at 773 K, the shear strength retained 74 MPa (only 16% degradation), ranking among the highest reported for thermoelectric materials/metal joints. Exceptional damage-tolerance of a medium-entropy alloy CrCoNi at cryogenic temperatures

Abstract: High-entropy alloys are an intriguing new class of metallic materials that derive their properties from being multi-element systems that can crystallize as a single phase, despite containing high concentrations of five or more elements with different crystal structures. Here we examine an equiatomic medium-entropy alloy containing only three elements, CrCoNi, as a single-phase face-centred cubic solid solution, which displays strength-toughness properties that exceed those of all high-entropy alloys and most multi-phase alloys. At room temperature, the alloy shows tensile strengths of almost 1 GPa, failure strains of ∼70% and KJIc fracture-toughness values above 200 MPa m1/2; at cryogenic temperatures strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength levels above 1.3 GPa, failure strains up to 90% and KJIc values of 275 MPa m1/2. Such properties appear to result from continuous steady strain hardening, which acts to suppress plastic instability, resulting from pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning. Magnetically-driven phase transformation strengthening in high entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractCrCoNi alloy exhibits a remarkable combination of strength and plastic deformation, even superior to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy. We connect the magnetic and mechanical properties of CrCoNi, via a magnetically tunable phase transformation. While both alloys crystallize as single-phase face-centered-cubic (fcc) solid solutions, we find a distinctly lower-energy phase in CrCoNi alloy with a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure. Comparing the magnetic configurations of CrCoNi with those of other equiatomic ternary derivatives of CrMnFeCoNi confirms that magnetically frustrated Mn eliminates the fcc-hcp energy difference. This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy, and is triggered by dislocation slip and interaction with internal boundaries. This phase transformation sets CrCoNi apart from the parent quinary, and its other equiatomic ternary derivatives, and provides a new way for increasing strength without compromising plastic deformation. Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Co32Cr28Ni32.94Al4.06Ti3 High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: High-entropy alloys have good application prospects in nuclear power plants due to their excellent mechanical properties and radiation resistance. In this paper, the microstructure of the Co32Cr28Ni32.94Al4.06Ti3 high-entropy alloy was researched using metallurgical microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and scanning electron microscopy. The mechanical properties were tested using a Vickers microhardness tester and a tensile testing machine, respectively. The results showed that Co32Cr28Ni32.94Al4.06Ti3 had a single-phase, disordered, face-centered, cubic solid-solution structure and was strengthened by solid solution. The alloy lattice parameter and density were estimated as 0.304 nm and 7.89 g/cm3, respectively. The test results indicated that the alloy had satisfactory mechanical properties with yield stress and tensile strength of about 530 MPa and 985 MPa, respectively.
